scene-u01-pnew1-5.name: text#5
scene-u01-pnew1-5.text: Each state emission density is a weighted sum of three Gaussians; each point comes from some component

scene-u01-pnew1-6.name: text#6
scene-u01-pnew1-6.text: How to read: dashed curves are components times mixing weights, the black curve is their sum (emission density), red dots are two points for responsibilities; the right splits $\gamma_k(i,m)$ into two layers and computes both responsibilities.

scene-u01-pnew1-52.name: text#52
scene-u01-pnew1-52.text: Dashed: component times weight; black: their sum

scene-u01-pnew1-56.name: text#56
scene-u01-pnew1-56.text: Mixing weights must satisfy $\sum_{m}c_{im}=1$ so the density integrates to $1$.

scene-u01-pnew1-73.name: text#73
scene-u01-pnew1-73.text: Responsibilities: blue comp. 1, orange comp. 2, green comp. 3

scene-u01-pnew1-82.name: text#82
scene-u01-pnew1-82.text: Responsibilities: blue comp. 1, orange comp. 2, green comp. 3

scene-u01-pnew1-86.name: text#86
scene-u01-pnew1-86.text: At $x=2.0$, component $2$ gets $0.5092$ and component $3$ gets $0.4908$: nearly half each, hard to tell apart.

scene-u01-pnew1-88.name: text#88
scene-u01-pnew1-88.text: Density and responsibilities by code, checked

scene-u01-pnew2-5.name: text#5
scene-u01-pnew2-5.text: Ambiguous observation $0.2$: soft splits it between states, hard gives it all to state $2$

scene-u01-pnew2-6.name: text#6
scene-u01-pnew2-6.text: How to read: two bars under each observation are its weight for state 1 (blue: soft, orange: hard $0$ or $1$); the right computes the new means of both methods.

scene-u01-pnew2-8.name: text#8
scene-u01-pnew2-8.text: Weight of each observation for state 1

scene-u01-pnew2-39.name: text#39
scene-u01-pnew2-39.text: Vertical: weight for state $1$ ($0$ to $1$); the highlighted column lies between the two states

scene-u01-pnew2-43.name: text#43
scene-u01-pnew2-43.text: Soft and hard assignments nearly agree; the difference comes mainly from the ambiguous one.

scene-u01-pnew2-51.name: text#51
scene-u01-pnew2-51.text: $0.2$ counts $0.1675$ to state 1 and $0.8325$ to state 2

scene-u01-pnew2-57.name: text#57
scene-u01-pnew2-57.text: Best path $1,1,2,2,2$; $0.2$ goes fully to state 2

scene-u01-pnew2-61.name: text#61
scene-u01-pnew2-61.text: Paths are concentrated; soft splits the ambiguous point, hard picks one side.

scene-u01-pnew3-5.name: text#5
scene-u01-pnew3-5.text: Sharing Gaussians (tied-mixture) cuts parameters from $33$ to $17$; more components are not always better

scene-u01-pnew3-6.name: text#6
scene-u01-pnew3-6.text: How to read: bars count free parameters for three states with $4$ components each (gray: mixing weights, teal: means and variances); the right lists limits and a common myth.

scene-u01-pnew3-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew3-26.text: Mean and variance: $1$ each per component

scene-u01-pnew3-27.name: text#27
scene-u01-pnew3-27.text: Separate: $3+8=11$ per state, $33$ for three; shared: $8$ for $4$ components plus $9$ mixing weights, $17$ in total

scene-u01-pnew3-31.name: text#31
scene-u01-pnew3-31.text: Only the mixing weights $c_{im}$ differ by state.

scene-u01-pnew3-37.name: text#37
scene-u01-pnew3-37.text: "More components make a better model" is wrong: more components mean more parameters, unstable estimates and overfitting with little data; choose the number by validation.

scene-u01-pnew3-41.name: text#41
scene-u01-pnew3-41.text: A continuous model needs a density form first; Gaussian mixtures are common but not the only choice, and a wrong shape biases the model.

scene-u01-pnew3-45.name: text#45
scene-u01-pnew3-45.text: Each component has a mean and covariance; in high dimensions covariances have many parameters, so diagonal covariances or tied-mixture save them.

scene-u01-pnew3-49.name: text#49
scene-u01-pnew3-49.text: Gaussian densities approach $0$ far away, so scaling $\alpha$, $\beta$ matters more.
